HI I'm a Master's student in Artificial Intelligence and Data Science, passionate about developing innovative technologies that solve real-world challenges. My experience includes machine learning, deep learning, NLP, Python, React, and full-stack web development.

I've participated in several hackathons, including NASA Space Apps Challenge 2021 and 2024, where I gained valuable experience in teamwork, leadership.
summary: We developed ASTRA HEALTH, an AI-powered health monitoring prototype that helps astronauts understand how their health changes during long-duration missions. Crew members record physical and behavioral indicators, including resting heart rate, blood pressure, sleep, and fatigue, through daily check-ins. The dashboard shows trends against each astronaut’s personal baselines, while deterministic rules flag concerning patterns for review, such as declining sleep alongside rising fatigue. With explicit consent, Google Gemini explains the recorded findings in plain language, answers personalized questions, and helps compile a daily report with suggested follow-up checks. Curated NASA references provide context for those explanations. By making changes easier to recognize and discuss, ASTRA HEALTH aims to support astronaut health awareness and autonomy when communication with Earth is delayed
details:
Long-duration missions expose astronauts to microgravity, space radiation, isolation and confinement, and the stresses of living in a closed spacecraft environment. Distance from Earth can delay communication and limit access to medical support and resupply. Crews need a practical way to see how their health changes over time, identify patterns worth reviewing, and share a clear account of those changes with medical teams. NASA Human Research Program

ASTRA HEALTH brings daily health tracking and an AI assistant into one workspace. It helps an astronaut answer three practical questions. What changed relative to my usual readings? What should I pay attention to? What should I record or recheck before the next review? A separate, read-only demo illustrates stable readings, disrupted sleep with fatigue, and rising resting heart rate alongside reported symptoms. All three scenarios use synthetic data.

Astronauts register and sign in to a private account, then enter mission information and set their personal baselines. During daily check-ins, they manually record resting heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, oxygen saturation, sleep, mood, stress, fatigue, and exercise. They can add notes about symptoms and well-being. The form validates measurements and allows missing readings. The dashboard displays the latest values, baseline differences, and interactive historical charts.

The backend compares the latest readings with any baselines the astronaut has set. For recent trends, it compares the mean of the latest three valid readings with the mean of earlier valid readings among the last seven check-ins, provided there are at least four valid readings. Configurable rules flag significant deviations, missing measurements, and stale check-ins. A combination such as reduced sleep and elevated fatigue can trigger a crew-review flag. These thresholds are for demonstration.

When an astronaut consents and requests cloud AI, the backend sends recent check-ins, calculated trends, alerts, and relevant reference summaries to Google Gemini. The health analysis describes observed changes, possible contributing factors, and follow-up checks. The chatbot uses the same context to answer questions about the astronaut’s records or relevant spaceflight health topics. The downloadable daily report combines recorded measurements, trends, and existing alerts with generated explanations. The backend selects sources from a curated collection of NASA Human Research Program materials and resolves returned citations against that collection.

The interface uses React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Recharts. A Python FastAPI backend handles validation, analysis, and access to SQLite through SQLAlchemy. The assistant calls an existing Gemini model through Google’s official Python SDK and validates the structured response. The team uses Gemini as an API integration without custom model training.

The personal baseline gives each alert context. For example, an astronaut can see how far sleep duration has moved from their usual value and whether fatigue rose over the same period. The chart shows the underlying readings, the rule identifies the combination that triggered review, and the assistant explains the pattern in everyday language. NASA references give crew members a way to explore relevant spaceflight research.

Argon2id hashes passwords, and HttpOnly cookies carry opaque tokens for expiring server-side sessions. The backend scopes private readings and AI history to the authenticated account. Explicit consent is required before health context goes to Gemini. Alert calculations run independently of AI-generated explanations. Check-ins, charts, and alerts work without internet while the local server is reachable. Gemini features require an internet connection and a configured API key.

On future deep-space missions, this approach could help crews notice changes earlier, make more informed self-assessments, and prepare better questions for medical consultations. ASTRA HEALTH is a research prototype with manually entered data and demonstration alert rules. Future work includes connecting wearable sensors, evaluating on-device AI for disconnected operations, and developing mission-specific review and escalation protocols in collaboration with medical experts. Clinical validation, security hardening, and testing under mission conditions are prerequisites for operational use.
dataRefs: NASA  Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight
